questions.q: Show me your GitHub repositories.
questions.followup: Why did you build this one, and what would you do differently today?

questions.q: Show me websites you have created.
questions.followup: Why did you choose that tech stack and hosting?

questions.q: Show me the tools you use.
questions.followup: Why these tools over the alternatives?

questions.q: Show me the AI skills and extensions you have installed.
questions.followup: Why did you need each one, and how did it change the way you work?

questions.q: Show me something you automated.
questions.followup: Why was it worth automating, and how much time or effort does it save?

questions.q: Show me a chatbot you built.
questions.followup: Why did you design it that way, and how do you handle wrong answers?

questions.q: Tell me about a project you are proud of.
questions.followup: Why are you proud of it, and what was the hardest part?

questions.q: Have you been part of creating an AI strategy?
questions.followup: Why did the organization need it, and how was success measured?

questions.q: Have you been a project manager on an AI project?
questions.followup: Why did the project succeed or struggle, and what did you learn?

questions.q: Can you recall some recent AI news you read or explored?
questions.followup: Why does it matter, and how could it affect our business?

questions.q: Is there a feature, product, tool or invention you really admire?
questions.followup: Why that one over the others, and how would you improve it?

questions.q: How do you use AI in your day-to-day work?
questions.followup: Why do you trust its output, and how do you check it?

questions.q: What is the difference between a graph database and a vector database?
questions.followup: Why would you use both together in one AI system, for example in GraphRAG?

questions.q: Have you used Hugging Face, and how?
questions.followup: Why did you choose those models, datasets or Spaces, and how did you evaluate them?

questions.q: What is LangChain, and how do LangGraph and LangSmith fit with it?
questions.followup: When would you skip LangChain and call the model API directly, and why?

questions.q: Name the main parts of the Hugging Face ecosystem (for example Hub, Spaces, Transformers, Datasets, PEFT, TGI, smolagents) and what each is for.
questions.followup: How would you take an open model from the Hub to a production API?

questions.q: What is Liquid AI, and how are its Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs) different from Transformer LLMs?
questions.followup: When would you pick a small on-device model like LFM2 over a large cloud model such as GPT or Claude?

questions.q: What kinds of decision models do you know (rules and decision tables, decision trees, ensembles, expected utility, MDPs, multi-criteria), and when would you use each?
questions.followup: How would you explain a model's decision to a regulator or an affected customer?

questions.q: How do you turn a model's prediction into a business decision, for example choosing the threshold for a fraud or loan model?
questions.followup: When should a human review the decision, and how would you check it for bias?

questions.q: What is FLOPS?
questions.followup: Why can peak FLOPS be misleading when choosing a GPU for LLM inference?

questions.q: What chunking strategies or approaches do you know for RAG (for example fixed-size, recursive, sentence- or document-structure-based, semantic, overlap, parent-child)?
questions.followup: Why would you choose one chunking strategy over another, and how do chunk size and overlap affect retrieval quality and cost?

questions.q: What are the different types of RAG architectures and strategies (for example naive RAG, advanced RAG with re-ranking and query rewriting, hybrid search, GraphRAG, agentic RAG, multimodal RAG)?
questions.followup: Why would you pick a particular RAG architecture for a use case, and how would you evaluate whether it works?

questions.q: What is MCP (Model Context Protocol) and how does it work: hosts, clients and servers; tools, resources and prompts?
questions.followup: Why use MCP instead of building a custom integration for every tool, and what security risks does it bring?

questions.q: What is an AI agent, and which agent patterns do you know (ReAct, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer, multi-agent handoffs)?
questions.followup: Why and when would you choose a simple fixed workflow over a fully autonomous agent?

questions.q: How do you evaluate an LLM application (evals)?
questions.followup: Why can't you rely on public benchmarks alone, and how do you make sure an LLM-as-a-judge is trustworthy?

questions.q: Which benchmarks do you know for LLMs and for AI hardware, and what does each one measure?
questions.followup: Why can benchmark results be misleading (contamination, saturation, different setups), and how would you benchmark for your own use case?

questions.q: What is "Tron", and how does it relate to Project Maven, Google, and the Maven Smart System?
questions.followup: Why did Google walk away from Project Maven, and what does that tell you about ethics and employee pressure when AI is used for defense?

questions.q: Name a research paper that had a high impact on AI or generative AI, and explain what it contributed.
questions.followup: Why was that paper a turning point, and how does its idea show up in the AI tools you use today?

questions.q: What is the single guardrail rule that could eliminate the chance of AI eliminating humans?
questions.followup: How about the guardrail "protect humans at any cost": if all AI vendors agreed on it and applied it, would it be enough to completely eliminate the chance of AI eliminating humans?

questions.q: Talk about the EUV (extreme ultraviolet) lithography machine: what it does, who makes it, and why it matters for AI chips.
questions.followup: Why does a single supplier (ASML) for these machines matter for the AI hardware supply chain and for export controls?

questions.q: What is the difference between Git and a GitHub repository?
questions.followup: Why would a team use GitHub (or GitLab) on top of Git, and how do pull requests and CI/CD fit in?

questions.q: In a few simple steps, explain how to convert a website (web app) into a mobile app.
questions.followup: Why would you choose a PWA, a wrapper like Capacitor, or a full rewrite in React Native or Flutter, and what changes for app store review and device features?

questions.q: What is Ansible, and what is an Ansible playbook? Describe a playbook you have written or would write.
questions.followup: Does it work across remote servers, and how does it connect to them and run tasks on many hosts at once?

questions.q: Define these 126 AI and tech terms, grouped by area.
questions.followup: Why does it matter to explain technical terms simply to non-technical stakeholders, and which of these do you use most in your work?
terms: Computer systems that perform tasks normally needing human intelligence, such as understanding language, recognizing images or making decisions.
A branch of AI where systems learn patterns from data instead of being explicitly programmed with rules.
Machine learning with neural networks of many layers, which learn features directly from raw data.
AI that creates new content such as text, images, audio, video or code.
The field of AI focused on understanding and generating human language.
Hypothetical AI that matches or exceeds humans across most cognitive tasks.
A model of connected layers of artificial neurons; each connection has a weight that is adjusted during training.
The algorithm that computes how much each weight contributed to the error by passing gradients backward through the network.
An optimization method that updates weights step by step in the direction that reduces the loss.
A formula that measures how wrong the model's predictions are; training tries to minimize it.
How big each weight update is during training; too high is unstable, too low is slow.
One full pass of the training data through the model.
The number of training examples processed together before one weight update.
When a model memorizes training data and performs poorly on new data.
Techniques (such as weight decay or dropout) that reduce overfitting by limiting model complexity.
Randomly switching off some neurons during training so the network does not rely on any single one.
A non-linear function (ReLU, GELU, sigmoid) applied to a neuron's output so networks can learn complex patterns.
A network using convolution filters to detect local patterns; the classic architecture for images.
A network that processes sequences step by step, carrying a hidden state from one step to the next.
A type of RNN with gates that help it remember information over long sequences.
The architecture behind modern LLMs; it uses self-attention to relate all tokens in a sequence in parallel.
A mechanism that lets each token weigh how relevant every other token is when building its representation.
An architecture with many expert sub-networks where a router activates only a few per token.
Two networks trained against each other: a generator creates fakes and a discriminator tries to spot them.
A generative model that encodes data into a probabilistic latent space and decodes samples from it.
A generative model that learns to turn random noise into data by reversing a gradual noising process.
A very large transformer model trained on huge text collections to understand and generate language.
A compact language model (usually a few billion parameters or fewer) that is cheaper and can run on devices.
A model that understands images together with text, for example answering questions about a picture.
A model that works with more than one type of data, such as text, images, audio and video.
A large model pretrained on broad data that can be adapted to many tasks.
The basic unit of text a model reads and writes, often a word or part of a word.
The component that splits text into tokens and maps them to IDs (for example with byte pair encoding).
A dense vector of numbers representing the meaning of a token, sentence or item; similar meanings have nearby vectors.
The maximum number of tokens a model can consider at once, covering input plus output.
A large, structured collection of texts used to train or study language models (corpora is the plural).
About meaning rather than exact wording; semantic search, for example, finds text with the same meaning even when the words differ.
A hierarchical classification scheme that organizes concepts into categories and sub-categories.
A formal model of concepts in a domain and the relationships between them, richer than a taxonomy.
The first, large-scale training stage where a model learns general knowledge, e.g. predicting the next token.
Further training of a pretrained model on a smaller, task-specific dataset.
Fine-tuning on instruction-response examples so a model follows user requests.
A fine-tuning method that freezes the base model and trains small low-rank matrices added to it.
Fine-tuning methods (like LoRA) that train only a small fraction of the parameters.
Training a smaller "student" model to imitate a larger "teacher" model's outputs.
Storing weights and activations with fewer bits (for example 8 or 4) to save memory and speed up inference.
Removing weights or neurons that contribute little, to make a model smaller and faster.
Artificially generated data (often by AI) used for training or testing.
Aligning a model using a reward model trained on human preference rankings, then optimizing the model with RL.
An alignment method that learns directly from preference pairs, without a separate reward model or RL loop.
A model that scores outputs according to learned human preferences; used in RLHF.
A design where humans review, correct or approve AI outputs or actions at key steps.
Making AI systems behave according to human intentions and values: helpful, honest and harmless.
Designing instructions and examples to get better, more reliable outputs from a model.
Asking a model to do a task without giving any examples.
Including a few worked examples in the prompt to show the model the task.
Having a model reason step by step before giving its final answer.
A sampling setting: higher values make outputs more random and creative, lower values more focused.
Sampling only from the smallest set of tokens whose combined probability reaches p.
When a model produces confident output that is false or not supported by its sources.
Retrieving relevant documents and adding them to the prompt so the model answers from them.
A database optimized for storing embeddings and finding the most similar ones quickly.
Splitting documents into smaller pieces for embedding and retrieval in RAG.
Search by meaning (using embeddings) rather than by exact keywords.
Combining keyword search (like BM25) with semantic vector search for better retrieval.
A second step that re-scores retrieved results with a stronger model to put the best ones first.
A network of entities (nodes) and their relationships (edges).
RAG that uses a knowledge graph of entities and relationships to retrieve connected information.
An LLM-driven system that decides its own steps and uses tools in a loop to reach a goal.
A model outputting a structured request to run an external function or API, whose result is fed back.
An open standard for connecting AI apps to tools and data through servers that expose tools, resources and prompts.
An open protocol that lets AI agents communicate and collaborate with other agents.
Curating everything that goes into a model's context at each step: instructions, tools, data and history.
The software around a model that turns it into a working agent: it runs the loop, provides tools, manages context and memory, and enforces permissions (for example Claude Code or Codex CLI).
Designing the agent loop itself: how the model plans, acts, checks the result and decides to continue or stop, including retries, feedback and stopping conditions.
Designing systems where many AI agents work together, each with a role, handing tasks to one another and coordinating to reach a shared goal.
Checks and filters around a model that block unsafe, off-topic or malformed inputs and outputs.
An attack where malicious instructions hidden in input or retrieved content try to hijack the model.
A prompt crafted to make a model ignore its safety rules.
A repeatable test that measures how well an AI system performs on a task.
A standard public test used to compare models or hardware (e.g. MMLU, SWE-bench, MLPerf).
Using an LLM to grade other models' outputs against a rubric or by comparing pairs.
How "surprised" a language model is by text; lower means it predicts the text better.
Using a trained model to make predictions or generate output.
The time from sending a request to getting the response (or the first token).
How much work a system completes per unit of time, such as tokens or requests per second.
Stored attention keys and values of previous tokens, so they are not recomputed at each generation step.
A processor with thousands of parallel cores; the main hardware for training and running AI models.
Google's custom chip designed for machine learning.
A chip in phones and PCs designed to run AI models efficiently on the device.
NVIDIA's platform and programming model for running general-purpose computation on its GPUs.
A unit in NVIDIA GPUs specialized for fast matrix multiply-accumulate, the core math of deep learning.
Stacked memory placed next to the GPU chip that provides very high memory bandwidth.
NVIDIA's high-speed interconnect for direct GPU-to-GPU communication.
Floating-point operations per second: a measure of computing speed (lowercase "FLOPs" often means a count of operations).
Training or inference that uses 16-bit number formats for speed while keeping key values in 32-bit.
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company: the world's largest contract chip manufacturer, which makes most leading AI chips, including NVIDIA GPUs.
Dutch company that builds the photolithography machines used to manufacture chips; the only supplier of EUV machines needed for the most advanced chips.
A model whose trained weights are published so anyone can download and run it.

An open-source license that lets you use, change and sell the code, even in closed-source products, as long as you keep the copyright and license notices. Apache 2.0 also grants contributors' patent rights; MIT is shorter and has no explicit patent grant.

An open-source license that lets you use and change the code, but if you distribute software built on it you must release the combined work under the same license, with source code. AGPL also applies when the software is offered as a network service (e.g. SaaS).
A pricing model where the basic product is free and users pay for premium features, higher limits or business plans (for example ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini free tiers).
A defined way for software to request services from other software, such as calling an LLM over the web.
A set of libraries and tools that make it easier to build on a platform or API.
A text-based interface where you type commands in a terminal (for example Claude Code or git).
A free, open-source operating system family; it runs most servers, cloud machines and AI training clusters.
A Windows feature that runs a real Linux environment inside Windows, popular for AI and developer tools.
A compatibility layer that lets Windows programs run on Linux and macOS without a Windows license (the name stands for "Wine Is Not an Emulator").
The package manager for Node.js (JavaScript): installs and manages libraries and runs project scripts.
The package installer for Python: installs libraries from PyPI, e.g. pip install torch.
A command-line tool for sending HTTP requests and transferring data, often used to test APIs.
The programming language of the web: runs in every browser and, with Node.js, on servers.
A dynamic, readable programming language, best known for the Ruby on Rails web framework.
A high-performance programming language for scientific and numerical computing, with Python-like syntax and near-C speed.
A high-level Python web framework for building web apps quickly, with a database ORM, admin panel and security features built in.
A lightweight text format for structured data using key-value pairs and lists; the standard format for APIs and LLM structured outputs.
A human-friendly data format that uses indentation instead of brackets; common for configuration files such as CI pipelines and Kubernetes.
A simple text formatting syntax (# headings, **bold**, - lists) that converts to HTML; used in README files, docs and chat apps.
A powerful open-source relational database; with the pgvector extension it can also store and search embeddings.
Packaging an app with everything it needs so it runs the same way on any machine.
Red Hat's enterprise Kubernetes platform for building, deploying and running containerized apps (including AI workloads through OpenShift AI) on-premises or in any cloud.
A DNS record that makes one domain name an alias of another, for example pointing you.can-du-ai.com to husamalqawasmeh.github.io.
Cloudflare's serverless SQL database, built on SQLite, used with Cloudflare Workers.
Vercel's AI tool that generates web user interfaces and full-stack apps (React, Next.js) from a text prompt or image.
Practices and tools for deploying, monitoring and maintaining ML models in production.
When real-world input data changes over time from the training data, so model quality drops.
